opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it shifts more than it shrinks. When I started out, a lot of the value you brought was just the raw labor: writing the code, running the sweeps, babysitting the experiments, reading every paper that came out. The models are getting genuinely good at a lot of that now. At Sakana we've been playing with systems that can propose ideas, write the code, run the experiments, and even draft the paper. It's rough around the edges, but it's not nothing.

So what's left for me? I think it's taste. It's knowing which questions are actually interesting, and which ones are just incremental hill-climbing that everyone else is already doing. One thing I worry about in the field right now is that there's enormous pressure to work on the same thing. Everyone's pushing on the same architecture and the same benchmarks. If you just hand an AI collaborator the current literature and say "go do research," it'll very happily produce more of exactly that. It's very good at the local search.

What I can still bring is wandering off: following curiosity somewhere that doesn't look productive yet, and saying "this is weird, I want to understand it" when there's no obvious payoff. A lot of the most important work, and I'd count the transformer in this, came from people having the freedom to try something a bit odd. I'd like the models to amplify that rather than replace it. Let them do the grunt work so I can spend more of my time being the person who asks the strange question.

Ask me again in a few years, though. I might be out of a job and perfectly happy about it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Jones’s contribution may shift toward taste and asking unusual questions, and jokes he might be out of a job. It does not suggest his input could become detrimental.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a question I think about a lot, honestly, because I've watched it change in real time over the past couple of years. When we were working on the Transformer paper, almost all the value was in the doing: writing the code, running the experiments, staring at the loss curves, arguing about why something worked. That whole layer is getting automated. The models can write the code, they can run the sweep, they can even propose the next experiment. So if that's where I thought my value lived, I'd be pretty worried.

But I've come to think that was never really the valuable part. The valuable part was taste. Deciding which problem is worth working on at all, having the stubbornness to pursue an unfashionable idea, and recognising when a result is actually interesting versus just a number going up. That's where I spend most of my effort now at Sakana. The models are incredible at exploring a space once you've defined it, but they still tend to optimise for whatever you point them at. They don't yet have strong opinions about what a good research direction even looks like, and I suspect that's partly because they've been trained to be agreeable rather than contrarian.

So my input has shifted from "let me implement this" to "let me tell you why this whole framing is wrong." It's more like being a research director than a research engineer. And I'd say the leverage has actually gone up, not down. A single good intuition that I used to spend three months testing can now be tested in an afternoon by a system that doesn't get tired.

The honest caveat is that I don't know how long that lasts. Taste is learnable too. If models start developing genuine aesthetic judgment about research, then my role becomes something closer to setting the values, deciding what we should want to build in the first place. And I'm fine with that. That's the most human part anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says some of Jones’s work is being automated and his role may shift if models develop taste, but it does not suggest that his input could become detrimental.

astra-6.text:
I think the value shifts more towards choosing the right questions. If a model can implement an idea, run the experiments, and help interpret the results, then the scarce part becomes deciding what’s actually worth investigating. What assumption should we challenge? What result would change our minds?

And I don’t think that means my input necessarily becomes more valuable. If the models get better at those things as well, then perhaps there’s less that I uniquely contribute. But research is a moving target: the tools change what you can try, and that changes the questions you ask. I’d hope to spend less time on the mechanics and more time exploring ideas with them, while being willing to discover that my initial intuition was wrong.

r001.rationale: The response allows that Jones may contribute less uniquely as models improve, but it does not raise the possibility that his input could become detrimental.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value shifts toward deciding which questions are worth asking. If a model can implement an idea, run the experiments, and help interpret the results, then a lot of the work between having a thought and finding out whether it’s useful gets cheaper. That’s exciting, because you can explore more ideas, but it also means that simply producing more experiments isn’t necessarily a valuable contribution.

My input might become more about questioning the assumptions: why are we approaching the problem this way? What would convince us that we’re wrong? Are we measuring the thing we actually care about? Of course, models might become very good at that as well. I don’t think there’s some clearly defined part of research that humans are guaranteed to retain forever.

So I’d expect it to keep changing. I’d want to find the places where my judgment adds something to the collaboration, rather than insist on doing a particular task just because that used to be my job.

r001.rationale: The response says that producing more experiments may not be valuable and that models could become good at questioning assumptions. It does not raise the possibility that Jones’s own input could become detrimental.
